newsitem.title: USA: Clinton skewers liquor industry for ending ad ban.
newsitem.headline: Clinton skewers liquor industry for ending ad ban.

text.p: President Clinton on Saturday scolded the U.S. liquor industry for an "irresponsible" decision to drop a decades-old ban on television and radio advertisements.
"You're wrong to change your policy now," he said in his weekly radio address. "This is no time to turn back. Get back on the ban. That's the best way to protect all our families."

The liquor industry's trade association, the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, announced on Thursday it would end the voluntary ban on advertising of hard liquor products such as whisky and gin.
The ban had been in effect since 1936 for radio and 1948 for television. The Seagram Co. had begun defying the ban in June by running commercials for its Royal Crown whisky in selected local markets.
The four major television networks, CBS, NBC, ABC and Fox, have all decided not to change their policy against running liquor ads. Together the four own about 50 stations in major markets.
That left just under 1,200 commercial stations scattered across the nation not owned by the major networks that could be targeted by the liquor industry.
Clinton said it was "simply irresponsible" for the industry to expose children to such ads "before they know how to handle alcohol or are legally allowed to do so."
"I commend the four major broadcast networks for saying they continue to honor the ban and keep liquor ads off the air," he siad. "I urge all other broadcasters to follow that example.
"Parents have a hard enough time raising good kids these days, and all of us have a responsibility to help them to make those jobs easier, not harder," he said.
He said in the last year alone 2,200 young people between the ages of 15 and 20 died in alcohol-related car crashes.

Administration officials made some private appeals to the industry to maintain the ban. But because of First Amendment constitutional protections there was little recourse except for Clinton to use the bully pulpit of the presidency to rail against the decision.

Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt on Friday said he had no immediate plans to issue rules to block such ads. "That is a long, long and hard road to travel," Hundt said of the rulemaking process.

Clinton, whose war on tobacco cost him some support in the tobacco-producing states of North Carolina and Kentucky in his re-election, vowed that, "We must not weaken in this fight to protect our children from the dangers of tobacco."
He cited a report from the Centers for Disease Control that said more than five million Americans under the age of 18 who smoke today will eventually die prematurely from smoking.
Clinton in August announced strict rules to control tobacco sales and advertising to try to prevent youngsters from starting the tobacco habit.
